steps.title: This lesson's two questions
steps.text:
RECAP · SKIP IT IF YOU REMEMBER LESSONS 1–3
This lesson's two questions

You build a docs bot for your team's API. A user asks: “How often can I call search per minute?” The answer, 100, is only in your private docs. Make two guesses; chapter 4.1 answers the first, chapter 4.3 the second.

1. You send that question to a model with no docs attached. What does it do?

Answers 100: it learned it in training
Writes a plausible number that may be wrong
Always says it doesn't know

2. You add your docs and the bot answers 100 in a demo. How do you know it will keep finding the right passage after you change something?

Try a few questions by hand after each change
Keep fixed questions with known right passages; score every change
Trust the similarity score it reports

Pick an answer for each.

Go deeper

The first question is about RAG (4.1), retrieval-augmented generation: why the model needs your text in its prompt. The second is about evals (4.3): measuring the system instead of eyeballing it.

Skip recap →

steps.title: Closed book: the model guesses a plausible number
steps.text:
CHAPTER 4.1 · STEP 1 OF 12
Closed book: the model guesses a plausible number

The model writes the next token from its frozen weights. With no passage in the prompt, nothing in the weights holds your limit, so the probabilities spread over plausible numbers. Put the passage in the prompt.

WHAT IT IS

A model answering closed book uses only its weights. Your private docs, and anything written after its training cutoff (the date its training text ends), aren't in them. Asked anyway, it writes the most plausible tokens, which can be a confident wrong answer (a hallucination).

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
A closed-book exam on a book you never read: you can still write a fluent answer, just not a reliable one. Open book, you copy the line.
Technical
A service answering from a stale in-process cache with no backing store: every miss still returns a value, so callers can't tell a miss from a hit.
Question only
Question + passage C2
Question: How often can I call search per minute?
Answer: You can call /search ___ times per minute.

probability of the next token (the number) · illustrative values

60
30%
100
26%
1,000
24%
10
20%

No single number wins: sampling (Lesson 2) picks one, and it reads just as confident as a right answer. That is a hallucination.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

The weights are fixed numbers learned from training text (Lesson 3). Your rate limit, 100, is in no training text, so no path through the weights favours “100” over “60” or “10”. Put C2 in the prompt and the same frozen model copies 100, because attention (Lesson 1: each token pulls in information from the tokens before it) reads it from the context.

EVIDENCE

RAG's original paper: pre-trained models “store factual knowledge in their parameters,” but “providing provenance for their decisions and updating their world knowledge remain open research problems.” Lewis et al., Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks (2020) ↗

Go deeper

A model can also say “I don't know”, if post-training (Lesson 3) taught it to when unsure. But it has no lookup to check against: it can't tell a fact it never saw from one it forgot. Putting the source text in the prompt is what makes the answer checkable.

steps.title: RAG: retrieve, then generate
steps.text:
CHAPTER 4.1 · STEP 2 OF 12
RAG: retrieve, then generate

RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) finds the passages most like the question, pastes the top k into the prompt, and asks the model to answer only from them. Change k, the number of passages sent.

WHAT IT IS

RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) has three stages: retrieve the passages most similar to the question, augment the prompt with the top k of them, then generate an answer that cites them.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
A librarian fetches the three most relevant pages, and you answer from those pages instead of from memory.
Technical
Cache-aside: on each request, read from the source of truth (the docs index), then render the response from what you read. The model is the renderer, not the database.
k (passages sent): 1

1 · Retrieve: every passage ranked by similarity to the question

#1	C3	Rate limits: the /upload endpoint allows 10 requests per minute per API key.	0.86
#2	C2 ★	Rate limits: the /search endpoint allows 100 requests per minute per API key.	0.84
#3	C4	429 Too Many Requests: you went over a rate limit. Retry after the Retry-After header.	0.71
#4	C5	Pagination: /search returns 20 results per page. Pass page=2 for more.	0.58
#5	C1	Authentication: send your API key in the Authorization header.	0.33
#6	C7	Billing: plans are billed monthly per API key.	0.29
#7	C6	E1042: your index is still building. Retry in a few minutes.	0.21
#8	C8	Webhooks: we POST events to your URL and retry failed deliveries for 24 hours.	0.17

Orange row = retrieved: sent to the model. ★ = the passage that holds the answer.

2 · Augment: the prompt the model actually receives

Answer using only these passages. Cite the passage you used.
[C3] Rate limits: the /upload endpoint allows 10 requests per minute per API key.
Question: How often can I call search per minute?

3 · Generate: 10 requests per minute [C3] ✗ wrong

Top 1 is the /upload limit, not /search: the passages are nearly identical. The model answered faithfully (it stuck to the passage it was given), but from the wrong passage. Chapter 4.2 shows why the ranking slipped.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Nothing about the model changes. Retrieval is a separate search system; its output becomes prompt text. If retrieval ranks the wrong passage first, the model answers faithfully from the wrong passage, as k = 1 shows: “10”, from C3.

EVIDENCE

The RAG paper pairs a generator with “a dense vector index of Wikipedia” and finds it generates “more specific, diverse and factual language” than the model alone. Lewis et al. (2020) ↗

Go deeper

Production systems often retrieve 20–50 candidates cheaply, then re-score them with a slower, more accurate model (a reranker) and send only the best few. Everything still ends as text in the prompt, so it pays the same per-token costs and the same prefill (Lesson 3).

steps.title: Chunking: cut the docs into passages
steps.text:
CHAPTER 4.1 · STEP 3 OF 12
Chunking: cut the docs into passages

Retrieval returns whole chunks, so the docs are first cut into pieces. Too small and a fact loses its subject; too big and one chunk mixes topics and costs more tokens. Change the size.

WHAT IT IS

Chunking splits each document into passages (chunks) before indexing. Each chunk gets one vector and is retrieved, and sent, as one unit. Overlap makes neighbouring chunks share some words.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
Cutting a recipe book into index cards: one card per step loses which dish it belongs to; one card per chapter makes every card about ten dishes.
Technical
Choosing a page size for pagination or a shard key: too fine and related rows split across fetches; too coarse and every fetch drags in rows you don't need.
6 words
12
24
48
No overlap
Half overlap

chunk 2	★	100 requests per minute per API key. The /upload endpoint allows 10
chunk 3		requests per minute per API key. Over the limit you get 429
chunk 4		Too Many Requests; retry after the Retry-After header.

★ = a chunk holding the number 100. Every word counts as one token here.

no
some chunk keeps “/search” with “100”
1
most topics in one chunk (/search, /upload, 429)

The fact is split: the chunk with 100 never says /search, so a search for /search can't match it, and a ★ chunk may even sit next to /upload.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Chunk size trades two failures. Small: the passage with “100” lacks “/search”, so it can't match a /search question. Large: one vector averages several topics, so it matches none of them sharply, and k chunks × size is what you pay per question.

EVIDENCE

Anthropic: traditional RAG splits documents into chunks, which fails “when individual chunks lack sufficient context”; chunk size, boundaries and overlap “can affect retrieval performance.” Anthropic, Introducing Contextual Retrieval (2024) ↗

Go deeper

Overlap repeats the end of one chunk at the start of the next, so a sentence cut at a boundary appears whole in one of them, at the cost of more chunks to store. Splitting on headings and paragraphs instead of a fixed count keeps facts whole more often. Another fix: prepend a one-line summary of the document to each chunk, so even a small chunk knows its subject.

steps.title: RAG, long context, or fine-tuning?
steps.text:
CHAPTER 4.1 · STEP 4 OF 12
RAG, long context, or fine-tuning?

Three ways to give a model your docs: paste them all (long context), retrieve a few passages (RAG), or train them into the weights (fine-tuning). Change the docs size and how often they change.

WHAT IT IS

Long context: put every document in the prompt. RAG: retrieve the best few passages per question. Fine-tuning: keep training the model on your text (Lesson 3's supervised fine-tuning) so the facts live in its weights.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
Bring the whole binder to the meeting, bring the three pages you need, or memorize the binder beforehand.
Technical
Full table scan vs an index lookup vs baking config into the binary at build time: the last is fastest per request but needs a redeploy for every change.
your docs, in tokens: 50,000
doc edits per week: 10
approach	answers from your docs?	input tokens / question	an edit shows up	shows its source?
Long context ← pick	yes	50,000	instant: edit the file	yes: it's in the prompt
RAG	yes	1,000	minutes: re-embed changed chunks	yes: cites the passage
Fine-tuning	unreliable for exact facts	~100	10 edits wait for a retrain	no

It fits, so pasting everything is simplest (prompt caching from Lesson 3 cuts the repeat cost). RAG wins once the docs outgrow the window or the per-question bill.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Long context: cost per question grows with docs size, and it stops at the window (128K in Lesson 2). RAG: cost is k × chunk size, whatever the docs size. Fine-tuning: no extra input tokens, but each edit needs a training run, and the model can't point to where a fact came from.

EVIDENCE

Comparing knowledge injection, “RAG consistently outperforms” unsupervised fine-tuning, “both for existing knowledge encountered during training and entirely new knowledge.” Ovadia et al., Fine-Tuning or Retrieval? (2023) ↗ For a knowledge base “smaller than 200,000 tokens”, Anthropic suggests skipping RAG and putting it all in the prompt. Anthropic (2024) ↗

Go deeper

Fine-tuning changes how a model behaves (tone, format, a narrow task), and that is where it shines. For facts that must be quoted exactly and change weekly, it is slow to update and gives no source to check. Teams often combine them: fine-tune for style, RAG for facts.

steps.title: Embed every chunk once, the question at ask time
steps.text:
CHAPTER 4.2 · STEP 5 OF 12
Embed every chunk once, the question at ask time

An embedding model turns each chunk into one vector, once, ahead of time: that's the index. At ask time it embeds the question the same way, and the nearest vectors win. Pick a question.

WHAT IT IS

An embedding model maps a whole passage to one vector (often 768–3,072 numbers) so that passages with similar meaning point in similar directions. The index stores every chunk's vector; a query embeds the question and returns the chunks with the highest cosine similarity.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
Shelving every book by topic once, then walking to the shelf that matches your question instead of reading every book.
Technical
Building a secondary index at write time so reads are a lookup: the expensive work (embedding each chunk) happens once at ingest; each query embeds one short string.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Same idea as Lesson 1's token embeddings, one level up: one vector per passage instead of per token. Indexing 8 chunks = 8 embedding calls, once. Each question = 1 embedding call + 8 cosines. For the /search question, C3 (/upload) scores 0.86, just above C2 at 0.84. The vectors capture “rate limit per minute” strongly and the endpoint name weakly.

EVIDENCE

Dense Passage Retrieval embeds questions and passages with learned encoders and beats “a strong Lucene-BM25 system largely by 9%-19% absolute in terms of top-20 passage retrieval accuracy.” Karpukhin et al., Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering (2020) ↗

Go deeper

The question and the chunks must go through the same embedding model: vectors from two different models live in unrelated spaces, so comparing them is meaningless. Swapping the embedding model means re-embedding every chunk.

steps.title: Keyword search, vector search, and both together
steps.text:
CHAPTER 4.2 · STEP 6 OF 12
Keyword search, vector search, and both together

Vector search matches meaning, so “call” finds “requests”, but it blurs exact words like /search or E1042. Keyword search matches exact words and misses synonyms. Hybrid search merges both rankings. Switch method and question.

WHAT IT IS

Keyword search ranks passages by shared words (rare words count more). Vector search ranks by cosine similarity of embeddings. Hybrid search runs both and merges the two rankings into one.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
Asking a librarian who knows the subject (vector) and also checking the index at the back of the book for the exact term (keyword).
Technical
Full-text search (an inverted index, like Elasticsearch) next to a similarity lookup, with a merge step that combines two sorted result lists.
How often can I call search per minute?
What does E1042 mean?
Keyword
Vector
Hybrid

#2	C2 ★	Rate limits: the /search endpoint allows 100 requests per minute per API key.	0.84
#3	C4	429 Too Many Requests: you went over a rate limit. Retry after the Retry-After header.	0.71
#4	C5	Pagination: /search returns 20 results per page. Pass page=2 for more.	0.58
#5	C1	Authentication: send your API key in the Authorization header.	0.33
#6	C7	Billing: plans are billed monthly per API key.	0.29
#7	C6	E1042: your index is still building. Retry in a few minutes.	0.21
#8	C8	Webhooks: we POST events to your URL and retry failed deliveries for 24 hours.	0.17

Vector score: cosine similarity. Top 2 retrieved.

Orange row = retrieved: sent to the model. ★ = the passage that holds the answer.

★ is ranked #2. The /upload limit edges out /search: the two sentences mean nearly the same thing.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Reciprocal rank fusion gives each passage 1/(60 + rank) from each list and sums. For the /search question: C2 is vector #2 and keyword #1, so 1/62 + 1/61 = 0.0325, just above C3 (vector #1, keyword #3: 1/61 + 1/63 = 0.0323).

EVIDENCE

Anthropic measured failed retrievals (how often the right passage was missing from the top 20 results): adding keyword (BM25) search to its contextual embeddings cut the failure rate from 5.7% to 2.9%, versus 3.7% with the embeddings alone. Anthropic, Introducing Contextual Retrieval (2024) ↗

Go deeper

The keyword score in real systems is usually BM25, a formula that rewards words that are frequent in the passage and rare across all passages. The merge here is reciprocal rank fusion: it uses only ranks, so the two lists' different score scales don't matter. Hybrid isn't free: in this lesson's test set it pushes one passage down (step 12 shows which).

steps.title: Approximate search: check a few regions, not every vector
steps.text:
CHAPTER 4.2 · STEP 7 OF 12
Approximate search: check a few regions, not every vector

Exact search compares the question with every vector: fine for 8 chunks, slow for 100 million. An approximate index groups vectors into regions and checks only the regions nearest the question. Change how many regions it checks.

WHAT IT IS

Exact (brute-force) search compares the question with every stored vector. An approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) index checks only a promising subset, trading a little recall (the share of true nearest neighbours it finds) for a lot of speed.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
Looking for the nearest coffee shop: you check your own neighbourhood and the next one over, not every shop in the city. Usually right, occasionally you miss one just across a border.
Technical
Partitioning a table and pruning partitions in a query: scan only the partitions that can hold the answer. A geohash lookup of nearby cells is the same move.
regions checked: 1 of 16

Teal dot = the question. Shaded squares = regions checked. Ringed = the true 5 nearest (exact search). Orange = the 5 nearest the index found.

25 of 400
vectors compared (6% of the work of exact search)
20%
recall: share of the true 5 nearest it found

The question sits near a region border, so some true neighbours live in regions it didn't check. Check more regions: more work, higher recall.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Exact search cost = number of vectors × dimensions. 100 million vectors × 1,024 numbers ≈ 100 billion multiply-adds per question, before any other user. Checking the nearest few regions cuts that to a few percent, and the knob (regions checked) sets the recall you get back.

EVIDENCE

HNSW reports “logarithmic complexity scaling” of search with the number of vectors. Malkov & Yashunin, HNSW (2016) ↗ ANN-Benchmarks plots every index as recall against queries per second: the same trade-off as the slider. ANN-Benchmarks ↗

Go deeper

Real indexes don't use a fixed grid. One family clusters the vectors first and checks the nearest clusters (IVF, inverted file index), exactly the knob above. Another, HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World), links each vector to its near neighbours in a graph and walks the graph toward the question. Both expose a knob that trades recall for speed. Internals are past this lesson's depth.

steps.title: Nearest isn't always relevant: a score floor
steps.text:
CHAPTER 4.2 · STEP 8 OF 12
Nearest isn't always relevant: a score floor

Vector search always returns its top k, even when nothing in the docs answers the question. A score floor drops passages below a minimum similarity, so the bot can say “not in the docs”. Move the floor.

WHAT IT IS

A score floor (similarity threshold) is a minimum cosine a passage must reach to be sent. Without one, top-k always returns k passages, because there is always a nearest neighbour, however far away.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
A search party that must return with someone: without a rule like “only if they match the photo”, they bring back the closest stranger.
Technical
A fuzzy match with no cutoff: a typo-tolerant lookup that never returns “no results” returns the least-bad match for every query, including nonsense.
How often can I call search per minute?
Do you support GraphQL?
score floor (minimum cosine): 0.50

#2	C2 ★	Rate limits: the /search endpoint allows 100 requests per minute per API key.	0.84
#3	C4	429 Too Many Requests: you went over a rate limit. Retry after the Retry-After header.	0.71
#4	C5	Pagination: /search returns 20 results per page. Pass page=2 for more.	0.58

#6	C7	Billing: plans are billed monthly per API key.	0.29 · below floor
#7	C6	E1042: your index is still building. Retry in a few minutes.	0.21 · below floor
#8	C8	Webhooks: we POST events to your URL and retry failed deliveries for 24 hours.	0.17 · below floor

Orange row = retrieved: sent to the model. ★ = the passage that holds the answer.

Bot: 100 requests per minute. [C2] ✓ right

The right passage clears the floor.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

For “Do you support GraphQL?” the best passage scores 0.41. With no floor, the bot gets three unrelated passages and answers from them. Floor 0.50 drops all three (“not in the docs”) and still keeps C3 0.86, C2 0.84 and C4 0.71 for the real question. Above 0.86, it refuses the real question too.

EVIDENCE

Models are easily misled by irrelevant text in the prompt: “the model performance is dramatically decreased when irrelevant information is included.” Shi et al., Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context (2023) ↗

Go deeper

There is no universal floor: cosine values depend on the embedding model, so the floor is tuned on test questions (chapter 4.3), including some whose correct answer is “not in the docs”. The prompt also tells the model to say so when the passages don't answer the question.

steps.title: A golden set: questions with known right passages
steps.text:
CHAPTER 4.3 · STEP 9 OF 12
A golden set: questions with known right passages

To know if retrieval works, write down real questions and, for each one, the passage that answers it: a golden set. Then count how often the right passage lands in the top k: recall@k. Change k.

WHAT IT IS

An eval (evaluation) measures a system's output against a standard. A golden set is a fixed list of inputs with known right outputs. For retrieval: each question plus the passage(s) that answer it. Recall@k = the share of questions whose right passage is in the top k.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
An answer key for a test you give the system: same questions every time, so scores are comparable across versions.
Technical
A regression test suite with fixtures: fixed inputs, asserted outputs, run on every change. Recall@k is the pass rate.
k (passages retrieved): 1

G2	C1 ★	How do I log in to the API?	#1	yes
G3	C6 ★	What does E1042 mean?	#2	no
G4	C5 ★	How do I get more than 20 results?	#3	no
G5	C4 ★	What does a 429 response mean?	#1	yes
G6	C8 ★	How long do you retry webhooks?	#1	yes

Orange row = its right passage was retrieved. Vector search.

recall@1

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Recall@k needs no model to grade: it is a lookup of where the right passage ranked. Here (vector search): ranks 2, 1, 2, 3, 1, 1. So recall@1 = 3/6 = 50%, recall@2 = 5/6 = 83%, recall@3 = 6/6 = 100%.

EVIDENCE

Hamel Husain on evals for LLM products: “Unit tests for LLMs are assertions (like you would write in pytest).” Husain, Your AI Product Needs Evals (2024) ↗ Anthropic reports retrieval quality as 1 − recall@20. Anthropic (2024) ↗

Go deeper

Why not just try a few questions by hand after each change? Hand checks vary from run to run and skip the questions that used to work, so a regression slips through; a similarity score only says how close a passage is, not whether it answers the question. Six questions are a toy: each one is worth 17 points, so one flip looks huge. Real golden sets start at a few dozen questions drawn from real user logs and grow with every bug found, and include questions whose right answer is “not in the docs”.

steps.title: Retrieval miss or answer miss? Score them separately
steps.text:
CHAPTER 4.3 · STEP 10 OF 12
Retrieval miss or answer miss? Score them separately

A wrong answer has two possible causes: the right passage never arrived (retrieval miss), or it arrived and the model didn't use it faithfully (answer miss). They need different fixes. Change k and the prompt.

WHAT IT IS

A RAG eval scores two stages separately. Retrieval: was the right passage in the prompt (recall@k)? Generation: is the answer right, and faithful to the passages it was given (no added or changed facts)?

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
A wrong dinner: either the shopper brought the wrong ingredients, or the cook ruined good ones. Taste alone can't tell you whom to retrain.
Technical
Tracing a bad API response: was the upstream data wrong (a bad query) or the rendering wrong (a bad template)? You log both stages to find the faulty one.
k = 1
k = 3
Plain prompt
Strict: quote the passage
Plain prompt: Answer the question using these passages.

Both kinds at once. Raising k fixes the retrieval misses; it can't fix G6, which had its passage and still said 48 hours.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Plain prompt, k = 1: 2 right, 3 retrieval misses (G1, G3, G4), 1 answer miss (G6). Plain prompt, k = 3: 5 right, 0 retrieval misses, and G6 is still 1 answer miss, because it had its passage all along. Strict prompt plus k = 3: 6 of 6. Each fix moved only the count it targets.

EVIDENCE

RAGAS proposes metrics for “the retrieval and generation dimensions” of a RAG pipeline separately, including faithfulness, and evaluates them “without having to rely on ground truth human annotations.” Es et al., Ragas: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation (2023) ↗

Go deeper

An answer that sticks to the passages is called faithful (or grounded). An answer can be faithful and still wrong if retrieval sent the wrong passage, like “10” from C3. That's why the two scores are kept apart.

steps.title: LLM-as-judge: grade free-text answers at scale
steps.text:
CHAPTER 4.3 · STEP 11 OF 12
LLM-as-judge: grade free-text answers at scale

Answers are free text, so exact matching fails on “100 requests per minute.” vs the reference. An LLM judge reads the question, the reference answer and the response, and grades it. Check every grader against human labels. Switch graders.

WHAT IT IS

LLM-as-judge: a model grades another model's output, given the question, a reference answer and a rubric (the pass criteria). It is trusted only as far as it agrees with human labels on a sample.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
A teaching assistant grading essays with the professor's marking guide. You spot-check their grades before trusting them with the whole class.
Technical
A fuzzy assertion in tests: instead of assertEquals on a string, a checker that decides “equivalent?”. You validate the checker on known pairs before it gates CI.
Exact match
LLM judge
LLM judge + rubric

Question G1 · reference answer: “100 requests per minute per API key”

human	grader	bot answer	vs human
pass	pass	100 requests per minute per API key	agrees
pass	fail	100 requests per minute.	disagrees
pass	fail	You can call /search about one hundred times each minute.	disagrees
fail	fail	10 requests per minute.	agrees
fail	fail	Limits vary by endpoint and plan; check your dashboard for the exact per-minute number.	agrees
3 / 5 = 60%
agreement with human labels

Exact match fails two right answers that are worded differently. It's only good for short, fixed outputs like a passage ID.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Exact match agrees with humans on 3 of 5 (60%), a plain judge on 4 of 5 (80%), the judge with a rubric on 5 of 5. The judge is a model too: same weights and sampling as Lessons 2–3, so it has blind spots, and grading costs tokens per answer.

EVIDENCE

Strong LLM judges reach “over 80% agreement, the same level of agreement between humans”, with measured “position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases.” Zheng et al., Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena (2023) ↗ Husain: correctness “is somewhat subjective, and you must align the model with a human.” Husain (2024) ↗

Go deeper

Five answers can't prove a judge works; real teams label 50–100 answers by hand, measure agreement, and fix the rubric until it is high. Known judge biases: preferring the first of two answers shown (position), longer answers (verbosity) and answers written by itself (self-enhancement).

steps.title: Lab: change one thing, re-run the golden set
steps.text:
CHAPTER 4.3 · STEP 12 OF 12
Lab: change one thing, re-run the golden set

Evals are a regression gate: a change ships only if it doesn't lower the score. Today's bot: vector search, k = 3. Try hybrid search or a different k and see if it passes the gate.

WHAT IT IS

An eval-driven change: run the golden set before and after a change, and ship only if the scores hold or improve. The gate can weigh quality (recall, judge pass rate) against cost (tokens per question).

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
A chef changing a recipe has the same tasters try the old and new dish side by side before it goes on the menu.
Technical
A CI gate on a benchmark: a performance regression test fails the build if p99 latency rises, even when every unit test passes.
Vector
Hybrid
k (passages sent): 2
id · right passage	rank with your setting	rank today (vector)
G1 · C2 ★	#1 ↑ better	#2
G2 · C1 ★	#2 ↓ worse	#1
G3 · C6 ★	#1 ↑ better	#2
G4 · C5 ★	#1 ↑ better	#3
G5 · C4 ★	#1	#1
G6 · C8 ★	#1	#1

Orange row = its right passage is in the top 2 now. ↑/↓ = ranked better/worse than today.

100%
recall@2 (today: 100% at k = 3)
700
input tokens per question (today 1,000)
$2.10
per 1,000 questions (today $3.00)
PASS
gate: recall ≥ today and tokens ≤ today

Same recall with fewer tokens: hybrid ranks every right passage in the top 2, so k = 2 is enough. Ship it.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Vector: recall@1 50%, @2 83%, @3 100%. Hybrid: @1 83%, @2 100%. So hybrid with k = 2 keeps 100% recall and sends 700 tokens instead of 1,000 per question: 30% cheaper, same quality. Hybrid with k = 1 fails the gate (83%).

EVIDENCE

Husain describes evals as a loop: write assertions, log traces, and use them to catch regressions with every change, like unit tests in CI. Husain, Your AI Product Needs Evals (2024) ↗

Go deeper

Look at G2 under hybrid: it drops from #1 to #2, because the keyword list ranks it last of the four passages containing “API”. An aggregate score can hide a per-question regression, so good eval reports also list which questions changed. A full gate would add the answer score from the judge (step 11) next to recall.

QUESTIONS
Check yourself

Answer each question out loud or in your notes before looking anything up. If one is hard, go back to its step.

1 · REVIEW · LESSON 3

Why does pre-training need no human labels?

2 · REVIEW · LESSON 3

What does the causal mask stop the model from doing during training?

3 · REVIEW · LESSON 3

Why does an output token cost more GPU time than an input token?

4 · REVIEW · LESSON 3

What does prompt caching reuse, and when does it hit?

5 · MECHANISM

Why does a model asked about your private docs produce a confident, plausible wrong answer instead of nothing?

6 · MECHANISM

Walk through the three stages of RAG for “How often can I call search per minute?”. What does the model actually receive?

7 · CONSEQUENCE

With k = 1 the bot answered “10”. Was the model unfaithful? Where was the bug?

8 · DESIGN

Chunks of 6 words vs 48 words: name the failure each causes, and what overlap fixes.

9 · DISTINCTION

Long context, RAG, fine-tuning: which would you pick for a 50K-token doc set? A 2M-token set edited daily? Why?

10 · MECHANISM

What is embedded ahead of time, what at ask time, and why must both use the same embedding model?

11 · DISTINCTION

Give one question where keyword search beats vector search and one where it loses. How does hybrid search merge them?

12 · NUMBERS

100 million vectors of 1,024 numbers: how many multiply-adds does exact search do per question? What does an approximate index trade for speed?

13 · CONSEQUENCE

What does a bot with no score floor do on a question the docs can't answer? What goes wrong if the floor is too high?

14 · NUMBERS

Right-passage ranks for six golden questions are 2, 1, 2, 3, 1, 1. Compute recall@1, recall@2 and recall@3.

15 · DESIGN

A wrong answer comes back. How do you tell a retrieval miss from an answer miss, and what fixes each?

16 · DISTINCTION

When is exact match a good grader, and when do you need an LLM judge? How do you know the judge can be trusted?

17 · DESIGN

Hybrid search with k = 2 vs vector search with k = 3: which ships, by what gate, and what could the aggregate score hide?

18 · BACKEND

Which backend patterns are RAG, the vector index, and a golden-set eval like?
